text: I'm a final year CS student at Bennett University. Last year I interned on a micro frontend dashboard in TypeScript and React, and I built Relay, which lets me control my laptop from my phone.
Nice. Tell me a bit more about Relay — what actually happens on the phone when you trigger something, and where does the Java side come in, if at all?

No Java in Relay, it's a Node agent on the Mac and a small web app on the phone. The phone sends a command over a WebSocket, the agent maps it to an action like AppleScript or a shell call, and streams the result back. The Claude API picks which action to run from plain language.
Got it, that's a clean design. What was the hardest thing you had to solve while building Relay — one specific problem you got stuck on?
Mostly my final year project, a scheduling tool for campus clubs, and polishing Relay. I'm ready for the coding part whenever you are.
Alright, let's get into it.

text: I'll take the scheduling tool then — that one sounds closer to real product work. What was the trickiest part there, the matching logic or handling the database side?

The trickiest part was conflicts. Two club heads booking the same room, so I used a unique constraint on room and time slot and handled the violation by suggesting the next free slot, instead of checking first and inserting, which raced.
Good, that's a real concurrency instinct — letting the database be the source of truth rather than a check-then-act. Let's move to the coding part now.

Sure. On Relay the hardest thing was ordering. Commands from the phone could arrive out of order after a reconnect, so I gave each command a sequence number and the agent drops anything older than the last one it ran.

Nice, sequence numbers on a reconnect is exactly right. Alright, let's start coding. I've put a problem on your screen — take a look and read it through. Think out loud as you go, and test your code before you call it done.

Reading it. So sessions are nodes, each prerequisite pair is a directed edge, and I need a valid ordering, so this is a topological sort. What should I return if there's a cycle, and can there be duplicate pairs?

There's no self-loops, and all pairs are distinct, so duplicates aren't a concern. For the cycle case, a valid full ordering won't exist — you should return an empty list. So, what's your approach here?

Okay. I'll use Kahn's algorithm. Build an adjacency list and an in-degree array, push every zero in-degree session into a queue, pop one, append it to the order, and decrement its neighbours. If the order ends up shorter than n there's a cycle, so I return empty. That's O of n plus e time and space.
That's the right shape. One thing to be careful about — when you build the adjacency list from a pair, which direction does the edge point? Convince me with a quick example.
A pair is a course and its prerequisite, so the edge points from the prerequisite to the course. For pairs 1 and 0, edge from 0 to 1, in-degree of 1 goes up, and 0 comes out first. Let me write it.
Good, that's the correct direction. Go ahead and write it.

Got it. Parcels stay in order, so I need the smallest capacity where a greedy day-by-day loading fits in D days or fewer. Feasibility is monotonic in capacity, so I can binary search between the heaviest single parcel and the total weight, and check each guess with one greedy pass. That's O of n log of total.
Yes, that's the right idea. Before you write anything, walk me through your feasibility check for a given capacity — how do you actually count the days?

Written. Test: weights 1 to 10 with 5 days gives 15. One day returns the sum, and as many days as parcels returns the max weight. Lower bound is the heaviest parcel so no parcel is ever stuck. Each check is O of n and the search is log of the sum.

Let me sanity check the day count on your cap of fifteen. Day one takes 1,2,3,4,5 which is exactly fifteen; day two takes 6,7 which is thirteen; 8,9,10 fit in day three. So three days, well within five — and eleven fails, so fifteen is the answer. Correct. Bounds are right too: heaviest parcel, and the sum for one day. Good job on that. Now let's talk about your projects. Can you walk me through how you architected the Next.js host shell and coordinated the Vite React micro-frontends in the Experience Portal?
Take your time — when you're ready, just give me the gist of how the host shell loads and shares things with the micro-frontends.

The host is a Next.js shell that owns auth and routing. Each micro frontend is a Vite React app exposed as a Module Federation remote, and the shell loads them lazily by route. React and the design system are shared singletons so we never ship two copies, and the shared login and token refresh live in the shell and are passed down through a small context.
That's a clean setup. Now dig into a decision for me — why Module Federation with shared singletons rather than just building the micro-frontends as separate npm packages the shell imports?

Versioning was the main risk. If a remote shipped a breaking change to the shared contract, the shell would break at runtime, so I pinned the contract in a shared types package and added a smoke test that loads every remote in CI before a deploy.
That versioning point is the real one. Let's switch topics for a minute — in Java, why must equals() and hashCode() be overridden together?

Sorry, on your earlier question: federation lets teams deploy independently, with npm packages every change needs a shell rebuild. On equals and hashCode: hash collections find the bucket with hashCode and then confirm with equals, so equal objects must share a hash code, otherwise a lookup in a HashMap can miss an entry that is actually there.

Both answers are solid — independent deploys on the federation side, and the bucket-then-equals lookup on the Java side. Let me go one level deeper on the micro-frontend. What happens when a remote is slow to load, or fails to load entirely — did you build any fallback for that?
I think that covers what I know on that one. I'm happy to take another.
No worries — I'd still like a quick answer on it, since reliability matters here. What does the shell show the user if a remote is slow, or fails to load altogether?

The shell wraps each remote in an error boundary with a skeleton while it loads, and a timeout after about eight seconds that swaps in a retry card. The rest of the portal keeps working because one remote failing never takes the shell down.

That's exactly the kind of thing that matters in production. That wraps up the technical side. Thanks for going through all of it — now let's turn it around to you. What questions do you have about the team or the work?
That's the floor to you then. Anything you'd like to ask me about the team, the way we work, or what the day-to-day looks like?
Nothing more on that, I think I've covered the main parts of it.
Thanks for your time. We'll share the feedback on the platform shortly, and you'll see the next steps there. Have a good day!
